Dense, tall building geometry narrows the sky view factor, so longwave radiation emitted by street surfaces is repeatedly absorbed and re-emitted by walls, reducing net longwave cooling and keeping the city warmer than the open countryside.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the sky is overcast and downwelling longwave radiation is uniformly high, the sky view factor ceases to be a differentiator between urban and rural areas.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If a city is highly dispersed with low building height, the street canyon radiation trap is minimized.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If wind speeds are high enough to mix the air, radiative trapping is overwhelmed by advective cooling.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The sky view factor determines how efficiently a surface radiates heat to the cold sky. In dense street canyons, the sky view is restricted, trapping longwave radiation. This reduction in radiative cooling creates a nocturnal UHI. The gap is larger in cities with deeper street canyons and greater building height, as the sky view factor decreases and the radiation trap intensifies.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
